title: India Just Had Its Driest June in Over a Decade. July May Not Be Much Better.
excerpt: The fifth-driest June since 1901, a strengthening El Niño, and a 23% lag in crop planting are raising alarms over food security and economic growth in the world's most populous nation.
body:
India's monsoon season has opened with a crisis.

June rainfall came in 39.8% below the long-term average, making it the country's fifth-driest June since records began in 1901 and the worst in more than a decade, according to the India Meteorological Department. And the forecast for July — the month that delivers the bulk of the season's rain — is not reassuring: below 94% of the long-period average, with El Niño expected to strengthen through the second half of 2026.

For a $4-trillion economy where nearly half of all farmland lacks irrigation and roughly half the population earns its livelihood from agriculture, the numbers are not abstractions. They are a countdown.

## The Planting Gap

Farmers have planted summer-sown crops on just 18.27 million hectares as of June 25 — nearly 23% less than the same period last year, according to Ministry of Agriculture data. The shortfall cuts across staples:

- **Rice**: 2.58 million hectares planted, down from 3.44 million a year ago. India is the world's largest rice exporter, accounting for roughly 40% of global shipments.
- **Soybeans**: 692,000 hectares, down a staggering 65% year-on-year.
- **Cotton**: 2.97 million hectares, a 35% decline.
- **Corn**: 1.57 million hectares, down 16%.

Sugar cane was the lone exception, rising 1.2% to 5.7 million hectares.

"The next 15 days are very crucial for planting most of the kharif crops," said J.S. Sandhu, a former agriculture commissioner. "There is definitely a worry while looking at water availability in our reservoirs and scorching heat."

## El Niño's Return

The El Niño weather pattern — marked by unusually warm sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific — contributed to the June deficit and is forecast to intensify. In most El Niño years, India has experienced below-average monsoon rainfall, and some have brought severe droughts that destroyed crops and forced the government to restrict grain exports.

IMD Director-General Mrutyunjay Mohapatra said below-normal rainfall is likely across most of the country in July, with the exception of some pockets in the northwest, northeast, and east-central India.

The monsoon had already arrived three days late in Kerala and then stalled for roughly two weeks over western farming regions. Some districts in the northern plains have been baking under temperatures above 42°C.

Only 9 of 36 meteorological subdivisions reported normal or above-normal rainfall in June. Gujarat's Dwarka district recorded zero rain for the entire month, against a normal of 100.3 mm.

## Markets Are Already Moving

The weak monsoon is rippling through commodity and financial markets. HSBC warned that while consumer staples firms are expected to post steady June-quarter growth, El Niño and a weak monsoon could hurt rural demand later in fiscal 2027.

Global rice prices have firmed on supply uncertainty, though high government buffer stocks — up 15% year-on-year at record levels for the start of June — are providing a cushion. A dealer at a global commodities trading house in Mumbai said adequate rainfall in the first half of July would be needed for farmers to take advantage of the remaining planting window.

The monsoon's performance also has direct implications for the Reserve Bank of India's interest rate calculus. A poor harvest season would push food inflation higher, complicating any move to cut rates even as crude oil prices have collapsed to pre-war levels.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs with family in rural India, the monsoon is not an abstraction. It determines whether the kharif season produces enough to sustain household income, keep food prices stable, and maintain the agricultural employment that supports hundreds of millions.

Remittance flows — India received a record $129 billion in 2025, the largest of any country — often spike during poor monsoon years as families in drought-affected regions turn to relatives abroad for support. If El Niño delivers a below-average monsoon, that pattern is likely to repeat.

Investors in Indian equities should also watch the rural demand story closely. Consumer staples, two-wheeler manufacturers, and fertiliser companies are among the sectors most sensitive to monsoon outcomes.

The IMD says a short-term rain spell is expected in the coming days that could provide enough soil moisture for delayed sowing. But the structural outlook — El Niño strengthening, reservoirs depleted, and 76% of districts reporting deficient rainfall — suggests India's agricultural heartland is in for a difficult season.

The monsoon has always been India's annual referendum on fortune. This year, the early returns are not encouraging.
